I will not go to war with my kin. I had hoped it would not come to this, but it was fated that no foreigner could solve such a dispute.
With their trust in you broken, it seems we are out of solutions. Dire times await. Sound the drums of war.
You are ready, and just in time. We have the upper hand, and must seize it lest it fades.
Underhanded, but efficient. Canons silenced by fire... Poetic justice, some may say.
Let these be the last of my enemies to die before me; I weary of blood. You shall be recompensed for helping restore Enbesan unity.
The Spear of Unity, for the one who wove that unity into being. A fitting gift, I believe.
The age of the Elamais ends, and with it go the remnants of that time. Take the Spear, and teach others of the tribulations of the Land of Lions.
Is this diplomacy to you? However dissident, the Princes of Angereb are kin to Enbesa, and I would have peace and unity with them!
Not the foundations I dreamed for Enbesa! Blood begets blood. But what is done is done, though I cannot say I am grateful.
Stay your hand— better an open door than a broken wall. There will be opportunities, I warrant to bring Angereb into the fold peacefully.
Restoring an ancient palace seems a small price to pay for peace. I shall send them my master builder.
There is a matter I would discuss with you, pertaining to the empire at large.
Enbesa stretches from horizon to horizon. Holding such a dominion is not an easy task, and there are those who yet oppose me.
Seek the heralds of Angereb in the meridian, and of Kidusi Anitoni and Waha Desher in the septentrion. Convince them we are better united.
Waha Desher! Once a land of bountiful wonders, torn apart by countless wars.
I once desired for Waha Desher to blossom anew, but that fruitless endeavour drains resources I can no longer afford.
There are writings housed in the library of Kidusi Anitoni that were old even before your Old World took to the seas.
But Kidusi's priests cling stubbornly to a faith long-forgotten, and will not join Enbesa until the day I decree their dogma the only Truth.
The pirates of Angereb deem themselves Princes, inhabiting the hallowed palace of the Elamais. But the lustre of its glories dulled long ago.
They refuse to bow to me, or any not of the Blood of Selamawi. Many times have I tried, but I cannot bring them to reason.
A time will come when we confront those who oppose Enbesa, but first must we tend to those who petition us daily for succour.
You have done well, brushing away the cobwebs on Kidusi. I have made arrangements— even a new monastery— so that the priests of Kidusi can join the rest of us under one faith.

You have worked wonders on Kidusi! Learning truth and tolerance, I have founded a temple here in Taborime, so that we can learn to be more inclusive of individual belief, for the greater good of the whole.
Good, you have taken Waha Desher by the scruff of the neck! In time it should thrive anew, with everything we have had to do for it. It could become a modern economic powerhouse!

You have breathed life back into Waha Desher! There is a natural beauty to it now, and many in this city have been inspired by their traditional example, raising gardens and terraces for all to revel in.

In your brave work on Angereb, you have uncovered facts about my heritage I didn't know myself! I have agreed, per Angereb's request, to raise monuments here to Hytia the trader and strengthen our newfound bonds.

You have done well to suppress Angereb. Peace is bought with might, so has it ever been. The new defenses of Taborime will ensure all know that Ketema the Builder shall be the bane of any who oppose him.
Beware the sweet words of the priests of Kidusi. They are cannier than they seem, and would see their faith vindicated rather than bow.
An interesting idea, but the capital will not grow if I expend workforce on secondary concerns.
Has the excavation yielded its secrets yet? Pray tell me if you require further assistance.
I have some machines here that would make short work of the excavation, and spare the labourers. Think on it.
The priests look to the past for guidance. A worthy stance, at times, but here... I fear it will mostly mean needless delay.
Take these shovels. May your labourers not suffer the pains of poorly wrought tools.
The past should be the soil for the seeds of modernity, not a burden to bear. The workers should not suffer only so that the dust of time remains undisturbed.

Long have we dreamed of that crossroads at which the knowledge of all the world can be shared. My adviser, Biniam, proposes a Research Institute, built in your Old World— a magnet for scholars from far and wide.
A mere trinket. Let them have it, and hold to your purpose. The sooner the excavation is complete, the sooner Kidusi will join the Empire.
I suspected there was more to this project than they let on. I sense underhanded ambitions to support their independence.
I take it things did not go as expected?
I had expected better than common forgery from priests. Evidently it is time they were brought back into the fold, and learned humility.
Lying in the face of an Emperor is crime enough, but lying before the Almighty... Kidusi is no longer the holy place it was. Let all know they are exiled, and their trade banned henceforth.
I would punish the priests for their lies, but people look to them for guidance. Very well — let them be united with the Empire. I pray, for their sake, this misguidedness does not renew itself.
Deliver this decree to Kidusi Anitoni, and let this tale come to a close.
I wonder, if they had been right, whether it would have changed anything? It matters not: our unity, our future, is now close at hand.
I have no need of subjects who would stoop to such deceit. This is my command: let none trade with Kidusi, nor grace their shores, nor mention their name. Let them be forgotten.
The stone must be destroyed. It is a symbol of lies and treachery, and emperils my dominion. I will see it ruined before it ruins Enbesa.
I am decided. Trade with Kidusi Anitoni will end, and they shall be left to comtemplate their decisions. Their island no longer exists to me.
Kidusi's independence I may allow, but the stone must be destroyed. What it stands for is perilous, and could be used to endanger my rule.
A letter from the High Priestess? I wonder what new deceit it brings — long does it seem since she spoke an honest word.
So all it took to make them see the beauty of change was the discovery of the remains of the past? The irony is precious, but their offer of unity is tempting.
They will kneel and pledge to the Empire as long as they are allowed to grow the sacred hibiscus? A small favour I shall happily grant!
Waha Desher expects a delivery. Take it to them, and in so doing, learn of their troubles.
So, Waha Desher. Is there hope to restore the island, or is it indeed a lost cause?
Water below, you say? Then we must bring it forth at once!
Change must come to Waha Desher. My patience and charity grow thin. They will adapt — or be abandoned.
Floods are certainly no menial threat. I can spare some trees from my land.
Do not tarry, time is short.
You have done much in little time. With water, Waha can surely now manage for themselves.
Festivals? More expenses! Time we made higher plans for Waha Desher.
Waha Deshans prefer to label me a demon than see my vision for them. Heed them not: the island must be made useful.
I respect the people of the wasi, but an Emperor cannot be expected to sacrifice so much for so little. They will join in the effort.
If you wish to help Waha Desher on their terms, then you shall bear the responsibility alone. It may thrive, or it may fade.
Are these not the people of Waha Desher?
Silence has claimed Waha Desher at last. It will be mourned, as beautiful things should, but perhaps it was for the best.
So ends the tale of Waha Desher. Trouble yourself not overmuch. You helped them as best you could.
I see you have good news! Let us have it then!
I had run out of patience, but you showed me the virtue of perseverance.
Ruins must be cleared to make way for the irrigation system. Doubtless the inhabitants will complain, but it must be done.
If you will not carry out my orders, then step aside. This is for the good of all.
Waha Desher has few resources. Wood and brick will be needed for the canals.
My men will clear furroughs and prepare the canals. Waha Desher will soon have its water!
The water now needs but a nudge of the hand, and a bountiful flood will flow forth!
Waha Desher an oasis once more! A place of beauty, growth, and trade. All Enbesa will turn to it as the future, and dream!
You know, Waha Desher still has untenanted land, that could be used to produce much of what Taborime needs.
Waha Deshan ceramics used to be famous. See that they are produced once more.
I appreciate your efforts, but their complaints stand in the way of progress. I will hear no more of it.
Waha Deshan cloth was also renowned. Enbesans will soon don raiment worthy of kings!
So Waha Desher at last ceases to be a burden on Enbesa, shifting its weight for the good of all. Splendid!
Never easy to be an agent of change — to erase the old and bring about the new. But nothing was lost in vain — gold glitters below the mire.
Not all change is an evil. With your help, Waha Desher can play a part in bringing Enbesa a brighter future.
I would greet our guest with a worthy gift: a comprehensive chronicle of our great land— the Epic of Lions! Come find me to discuss compiling it.
A fine scholar has recently returned from Vespuccia, where he was researching archeology. Find him in Kidusi Anitoni — he will be of great help.
Here, in the shade of my palace, shall you help me raise a new capital from the dust!
I wish to speak with you on matters of great importance, concerning all Enbesa! Will you work with me to help my people?
If you are to unite the many peoples of Enbesa, you must prove you can provide for them all.
Shepherds need only simple lodgings— most of their time is spent roaming the wilds with the herds.
Goods are but a fraction of what is traded. Tales, news, prayer — all are bartered freely around the stalls.
Wanza wood is sturdy yet versatile. To expand, you will need some groves of your own.
You may want to build these a little way off — noisome creatures tend to roost in the branches.
Already the lands grows at your command! Seems I am not mistaken in awarding you this opportunity.
Ours is a temperate way of life; we would rather warm goat milk than spirits.
Ah, the flavour of warm goat milk! A trying creature to herd, but so bountiful in its gifts!
Water is scarce in this region of Enbesa, but Biniam and I have been working on a system.
Water, much like people, is a primal force. But with willpower, with intent, it can be exalted for the good of all.
See how the land blooms? So would I see Enbesa blossom, and its people thrive.
It moves me to see our system at work... Ours is a culture of growing and nurturing — water, the key to bringing Enbesa together.
Traditionally, shepherds weave their own garments — but they need linseed, and linseed needs water.
It is my hope that all young people will, in time, come to Taborime to learn these crafts.
Enbesa is a crucible of cultures and people — but if we are similar in dress... it is a start towards unity.
Our children learn to hum before they can sing, and most of our liturgy is in song. Music defines us, as a people and as beings.
How they dance and sing! This is a legacy I would hand my people — a land of song and joy.
Best prevent any risk of fire — tapestries are, unfortunately, quite flammable.
Mind you ensure your fire station can readily access the channeled water!
Brave people these, who will stay the devouring flames!
This land you come from; I would know more of it?
How interesting. Certainly this should help prime me for diplomacy with your rulers.
Biniam tells me your lands hold many strange wonders. Would you care to enlighten me?
I confess, I had expected greater... eccentricity. Perhaps we are not so different after all.
It is not in vain the Almighty sends us dreams, but one mustn't forget the needs of those who live.
My people will travel far to tend to their duties. Thus, our food is often wayfood, salt-cured.
Many breeds of cattle roam Enbesa, but the sanga is best known, and beloved by all.
Not so long ago were the salt mines worked by thralls of the warring princes. I hope now they will stand for something better.
Pleasingly chewy isn't it? It may take a little getting used to for foreigners — as with many of our dishes.
The Elders have been clamouring for a place to partake in the holy endeavour. A testament to your stewardship!
Elders constitute a devout, opinionated group. Do not underestimate the reach of the Moot, their council.
The last tiles are inlaid, the drapes hung fantastical. Throw open the palace doors!
The pyre is lit — let leonine flame herald a new age for Enbesa!
The ancient baths are, sadly, rather overgrown. My wife, especially, is rather keen to see them restored.
Ah, what can bring a people together better than bathing blissfully together!
Singing goats? Did you drink too much tej? Very well, I shall give you the benefit of the doubt.
And they were singing, you say? Not bleating? Try coaxing it from them in melodic sequence...
Tell no-one I said so, but... I've heard court musicians less talented than these wonderful creatures...
And you kept a perfect bleat... But I'm afraid now we really must get back to work.
Oh! It seems to be a song about lions. Rather brave coming from goats.
It was only a matter of time before Enbesa attracted such attention. Now will its true test begin.
I am told you know each other. Pray welcome him in my name then, and see what wind bears him ashore.
A meeting? Very well, although I fear I know the outcome. Let us nonetheless be civil and prepare a banquet.
No banquet hall is complete if not suitably tapestried.
Such intricate work, soulful weaves... Pray send them to the palace, to be given place of honour.
There must be dishes aplenty — let Sir Blake know the bounty of Enbesa.
Let us see then what business brings Sir Blake to Enbesa. Come, your presence will be invaluable.
Weaving is ancient and noble craft. It requires natural resources that cannot be found on this island.
I hold no ill will toward Sir Blake. It takes time to accustom oneself to new surroundings. Bring him food, and he may yet soften.
Such fine aromas, crisp and full, the pale red flesh in heavy broth... A dish to reveal the hearts of men!
How thoughtful... Oh deary me, spices? That won't do — I'd be burning up inside like the Sixth Circle!
I hear Sir Blake is too poorly to explore the lands he lays claim to— it is the heat, surely. Shall we bring some of Enbesa to him?
He need not know our differences with these lands remain — unity soon shall mend us.
Angereb... There is beauty, and even some wisdom hidden here, behind those high and headstrong walls.
You call this progress as though it were one of only two paths to be chosen.
To attract such approval from the Irenya is no small feat. On such pillars will you build my capital.
Sir Blake is but one man, without allies and support here. He needs to see this for negotiations to resume peacefully and in good intent.
My heart sings to hear so many voices, to see so many colours! This is the Enbesa I dream of— united, yet strong in its diversity!
I had hoped much of our friendship in the Old World. Wrongly so, evidently.
Dark clouds gather near our borders. While I weary of warfare— the safety of my people comes foremost.
I had hoped Taborime would have no need of such beasts. I hope it still.
I gave you the choice to aid me willingly. How disappointing...
A dour offering, but we will have need of them, I fear.
Is this all Enbesa is worth to you? That you would abandon its people for the promise of trinkets?
I will give Sir Blake one last chance to repent. Bring him this gift— I am sure he will understand the message.
Be wary — the bees of Enbesa are kindly, but do not take to being mishandled.
Rotten fruit is the best he could do? Never mind, thank him, for this will feed the many poor families.
Deliberate? I will not believe it! Though it is not the first time men of the Old World inflict their sickness upon new lands. There have been precedents...
I had hoped you understood my people better. Clearly I was sorely mistaken.
I had hoped good counsel would make for peaceful times, but it seems I had neither. So be it. We must sound the drums of war.
In troubled times the people look to their lords, and to the Lord above, to provide solace.
You may need a different type of wood, perhaps from your homeland, for this.
How well I used to know these verses, studying every day in King Wag — my father's — chapel...
There are many beliefs in Enbesa, but only one Faith.
A letter has come for Biniam from his mother. You will go and explain to her how your recklessness put her son in danger.
If naught has changed by your return, the ships will sail to our foe in arms, and visit the wrath of the Empire upon him.
...but for you to appeal to Archibald's heart, Kirya, you must be able to reach him. I fear then, we have no choice but to carve you a path through the royal fleet.
Lives lost, ships destroyed, and for what? So a kinglet may make a mistaken point?
The way is clear, and time is of the essence! Kyria must be brought to Sir Blake before he settles upon retaliation he will live to regret!
I had a suspicion there was something, but this... Thank you for sharing, Elder Kirya. It may prove our salvation...
It is only fair that, those there at the start, be there at this new beginning as well.
A new start, new hope. There's wind in the sails again!
A wise decision, reminding Sir Blake of the deep and ancient roots of our land.
I thank you for presenting Enbesa as the powerful empire we know it to be.
I have much to thank you for — not least helping my subjects see the virtue of unity.
I need not say, I think, how much I owe. I will say only this: look to the skies today, see the glory of Enbesa united, and know that history will remember your part.
Scholars will need accommodation. Well-furnished yet small rooms— should stimulate an esprit de corps.
Janihoy Ketema, may I introduce my benefactor, a renowned city-planner from the distant north.
Our meeting was serendipity alone, my Emperor.
So must all stand to defend their share... or be eaten.
... Sail in and claim lands and people he has no right to...
... better to burn the crops than let these locusts grow fat on them!
The serpent rises true at last!
He is no father of mine, nor has he earned that title.
Then care for this land as much as you do her, and perhaps our peoples can still bond in sisterhood.
I have need of your advice to select an architect for a project I have been mulling over.
You see, it is my lifelong ambition to bring the world's great minds under one roof — a research institute, if you like.
Hmm. A dear and amiable bunch, but their work is small fry.
Talented, no doubt, but their experience too specific, their projects lacking scope.
Extensive knowledge, demonstrable skills... yes, this consortium have concepted the perfect prototype to become The Research Institute!
I know your people set much store by the history recorded in books, but the lore of Enbesa is too rich and storied to merely be read.
It must be seen, felt with sense and heart. Take in the land, its people, its past, and you will understand it like no other.
Ato Blake. A pleasure to make your acquaintance.
I am Biniam, Sir Blake, emissary for His Imperial Majesty and tasked with counseling him on this delicate matter.
A distemperate man if I ever saw one. And you say he is usually amicable? (thoughtful sigh)
Such different lands, united under one wise rule! How could anyone doubt the splendor of Enbesa now?
The learned men are wise, but wary of novelty. Take care not to startle them with your camera.
I was born here, in less happy times. It was rough sailing, but my mother and I took care of each other.
Kidusi has a joyous library — that's if you are clever enough to find a way past the priests.
There is much to do in Enbesa still, but such a wide world to learn from! Perhaps you could gather expert opinions in your travels, for my project?
Kyria my mother, lives on Waha Desher. As mother-son relationships go, ours has to be one of the best— except when she insists on those riddlesome Waha Deshan bond-words.
There are accounts of people all over the city falling ill to those fruit! This is no gift— it's an attack!
How could they not know, if there is a precedent? How could this not be deliberate— be murder?
So it is true then— there is no hope for peace, none for friendship... I suppose you have tried your best.
Have the people of Enbesa not suffered enough? There must be some other way — a compromise, a meeting...
Something must be done to drive that parasite, out of Enbesa—out of our lives— for good... The water! Of course...that's it!
Hurry then! I must get to the canals before first light — without them, the land will dry up, and Archibald will have no choice but to leave!
I wish harm on no-one, but we need time to prepare. I... Shall we, friend?
I will not have families torn asunder by one man's blind greed!
Now to find those pumps... Simple, harmless. None need be hurt.
He can't manage on this land without our help, yet he says we need him? We never needed him. Never!
There! Let the lycaon see how well he fares without water, we have no need of his arrogance and pride!
So many new horizons! This is the New Age of Enbesa, and we have you to thank for it!
You did it! This was forever my dream and now you made it true. Imagine now, how the world shall join hands in research!
We will need new facilities, an institute worthy of the world-renowned scholars desirous to push back the boundaries of knowledge!
An old classmate you say? Of course, I shall read it presently.
Hm. I have seen such characters before! A stone not far from where I grew up, tangled in the undergrowth.
It was atop a cliff. If you look to starboard from the camp ruins, there should be a narrow path through the cliff to a small dell.
It's fragmentary, but I'm confident this is part of the legendary Oathstone which marked Kashta's gifting of Waha Desher to Enbesa!
If I'm right — and I probably am — this is thousands of years old! Look — two texts, one in each language, so the treaty can be understood by all.
If it is the same text in two different languages, we could extrapolate a rough lexicon of the Ancient Script from our far more extensive knowledge of the Kashtan tongue!
Ah, yes, that does tie nicely to the context! Now what about this next section...
There must be some mistake. No language I know of would disregard basic grammar so violently. Let us start over.
Hm, yes, I see how that would make sense. Then that would mean that this last section is... Hm, not sure— any ideas?
Aha! We have it! The Lexicon Ya-Enbesa; a guide to the Ancient Script! Take it to the Scholar, he will be positively spitting for jealousy!
Hurry! Academic breakthroughs can suffer no delay; all must know of our work!
Ah, it's you! Please — my home is your home.
Come in, I'm working on a transoceanic research collaboration.
Could you bring the mail on your way in? I'm waiting on a research grant.
I want this international collaboration between universities to take off, but I also need to provide for mother.
It often amuses me that you should think of our land as a younger nation. If I read your scripture correctly, it originated in these lands, not yours.
A strange bond, between parent and child. I owe my mother so much but I do not wish to live in suffering as she has.
Scholars will need accommodation. Academics prefer modest quarters, with plenty of open space nearby to aid thought.
Archibald. I want to say you look well, but... Exertion does not become you.
Release him, Archibald.
Awo, Biniam is my boy.
He only saw me, Archibald. He did not see you — for many years.
Biniam, is that you? Oh, my apologies, I thought you were my son. And you would be?
Honesty is a virtue, however painful the truth may be.
Lies are the Deceiver's tools, child. Never suffer them to use your tongue, whatever the reason!
The roots are deep; make sure to sift through the earth to clear it all, will you?
I kept a diary of sorts when I was younger, before... Before Biniam was born. You may find it of interest.
The truth is an orange, sour-skinned and pithy. Sharpen your blade, and when ready, peel it open.
So Biniam knows...I had thought it best to keep it from him, all those years— keep him safe. Besides, they paid me to keep quiet about it...
The money they paid me to keep silent afforded Biniam an education, a place in the world. Was I wrong to choose to give him a future rather than a past?
Janihoy Ketema. I do not know how to put this...I knew Sir Archibald— before. He and I were in love once. Biniam is the product of that union.
I have little, but you are welcome to it nonetheless.
Come out of the sunlight; I'll brew you some tea.
There used to be entire groves of orange trees on these hills in my youth.
Ah Biniam!— No matter if he be tall, or his hair going grey, he will always be a boy in his mother's heart.
I learned plant-lore from my wahiyit, as she from hers before. Come, let me show you.
Land-healing relies on the nurture of plants — orange issehds, croplands, dark issehds. But the waha is dry and needs more.
That's enough to seed the waha with new life. Come, I will show you the apportioned place for each plant.
To see such verdant life... Biniam did not love growing as I do, but I believe he would agree we have done good here.
Waha Desher is a haven of peace, a place of quiet! No industry should marr the bated stillness of a garden!
...maintain the position Her Majesty set out in her letter...
...use any means at hand to achieve the necessary result... a personal failure would be unacceptable...
...I swore to myself I'd never return — swore it!
Wha- How? You? And why are you here...?
Ah, yes of course! Yes, of course — Her Majesty has no qualms with free traders...
...but please, no politicking here, for the Crown has a vested interest in Enbesa.
Is this the hospitality of Enbesa — flames and steel in the night? Seize him, and see to his extradition!
I want him as far away as possible. Slate him for transportation to New Holland, along with the other criminals.
And who are you, o king, to countermand the will of Empire? I fear our talk must now be of fleets and steel!
...K-Kyria?
It is you... Those quizzical eyes — how could I forget?
Him? You mean...
Not... not Biniam? He can't be...
The prisoner is to receive a full pardon. Return his possessions, we go to meet the Emperor.
Janihoy Ketema, there will be no war between us, for the truth is I have no quarrel with any here, save myself.
I have all along had power to do great good here, yet was distracted, and upset... by matters personal.
I do not ask your forgiveness Biniam... but perhaps in time...
...how often I wondered, yearned...But I never could...and I regret it, I regret it...
No-one could ever have replaced either of you...
...But I poured all that terrible guilt with constancy into Her Majesty's nurture and protection...
And that is why, Kiburi Biniam; most patient Emperor Ketema...
...I will make the necessary arrangements for a swift departure...
...and open myself up to negotiations between our people, may Her Majesty hang me for it.
Ah, I knew I'd forgotten something! I'll prop a registry up in a jiffy!
Pyrphorians in Enbesa you say...? Perhaps we should bait them with a mock royal visit?
Since you have had time to reconnoitre, I wonder if you couldn't help me with some blanks on our survey maps?
It's a real bugger what with the heat and the terrain, but the idea is we name every landmark we stumble across.
Ah, well spotted. Oh dear, that little elephant has become separated from its herd...
When clearly they want help, intervention is hard to resist. We'll class this site 'Elephant Grave Theta".
Ah! The maned head of the animal state. There is but one true King... or Queen.
The Queen will appreciate that image. Let us map this 'Lionheart Spur'.
Ah yes these falls...I remember...bored, we were...drank terribly only nearby...
Just empties...
Uninteresting.
Ah! A vintage whisky that might provide me some relief. Ha! Let's name this 'Scotch Falls.'
What!? An arch, like a finishing post? Perhaps we should dash a frivolous furlong or two?
And I'd have bet on you for that derby! Well, indeed, I think now I have the honour of naming it 'Blake's Archie'.
Good on you! Always were a thoroughbred, indeed, indeed. We'll name the arch 'Victory Bow".
That's all of the major landmarks— you realise you have done the Queen a vital service…
...accurate cartography is of great importance to the empire, if we really are to master the country.
I don't suppose there are fountains? No? Well... perhaps some of those water-furrows then?
Cool water would mollify him for further entreaties.
Not even an orange tree to shelter under— come now and don't dither!
So swift to learn from those who came before... Let us hope he proves grateful.
Is that really all there is to it? Pish, better than roasting to a cheltam-salt crisp!
Time to saddle up? Very well, lead the way— a familiar face ought to put the "king" in a good disposition.
Morning winds on the rise, eh? Ominous, ominous indeed.
Sir Archibald will do, my good man — your Emperor will be expecting me.
Ah, a familiar face! Splendid! Come now, take me to this Ketema — we have much to discuss.
He should know of me already — I wrote often enough, but communications in this land seem haphazard.
Outrageous! Arrogant! How dare he think himself an equal to Her Majesty? Pompous little kinglet...
Of all the useless... Why did I ever agree to come back to these wretched shores? It's pointless.
An explorer with no maps! (scoffs) It's like a ship with no topsails!
Natural beauty, certainly! But Her Majesty did not send me here to sightsee. She has great hopes that Enbesa might fall in and become a powerful industrial cog.
Elders wield a great power in Enbesan society— their Moot respected and obeyed. Convincing some to join you would support Her Majesty's designs here.
Further expansion? This will not do at all— stem the tide! Her Majesty greatly appreciates, and rewards, loyalty.
It gives me no pleasure to make these people miserable, but it is temporary. They will be better under Her Majesty's stewardship in the end.
See how he gathers for war? Hospitality of Enbesa, I'll say... Bring me the cannons and I'll reward you handsomely.
Biniam is strangely glad you chose Archibald, even if he tries to pretend he is disappointed.
Wonderful! I knew you were a stout and reliable sort!
I... I see. How kind. Please take these away— somewhere distant, preferably.
The mighty Ketema extends a sign of goodwill? My memory of him is not of someone so reasonable.
If this King is going to behave like a spoiled child, then I'll give him a piece of my own mind.
I... I had no knowledge of this! It was an accident. I would never stoop to such underhanded ways!
There is fruit enough here for all Ketema's people, sent in from the Old World — the long way.
I meant approval for Her Majesty's Empire, not Ketema's... (tired sigh). Confound it, why was I not informed of this?
Ketema's supposed might! Mercenaries abound who will defend me, and before long Her Majesty's navy will be here in full force!
You proved your loyalty. To these lands, to truth, to peace, and most importantly, to Her Majesty!
Her Majesty will be delighted with the wealth of knowledge I bring back— maps, legends etc. One good excuse I'll have for her anyway...
Troubled times make familiar faces friendly, eh? Well there's always a berth on Her Majesty's land if you want to feel more at home.
All the arrangements are made— not a trace left on the island. Escort me before Emperor Ketema once more, I am ready to negotiate.
I should have known better than to fear and deny the past— to lie to others, lie to myself. Only the worst of politicians would do that.
An excavation, you say? Capital idea! Her Majesty will be delighted to add some exotic artefacts to her collections!
Ah, right, yes... a suspenders-only sort of day, isn't it?
Ah, right, yes... What-ho! Just in time for a spot of water polo!
You managed to scare all the birds off with your landing...
A chap in my command once tried to duel an oryx with his sabre, and lost. Nasty temper they have.
A young man has dignity until he rides a camel. Then it's all about getting back at the brute.

You dock at a small, lively port on the northern coast. While most of your crew replenish supplies and repair the damage suffered in a recent storm, some decide to head off to explore the local souq.

Streets fold and unfold into each other, bedecked in a wild array of colours and dizzyingly heady unknown scents, which so confuse your sailors that they become lost in the weave of passages. Seeing their distress, several young men in beggarly clothes offer to guide them through the maze.
Shoo them off and trust your crew’s instincts.

It takes some observation, but your sailors soon understand that the mosaic of low-hanging cloths are arranged in specific patterns. A sharp right after a spice dealer’s enthusiastic attempt to sell your crew a few years’ worth of ochre and red powders leads them to a small, shadowed plaza, where two musicians are strumming many-stringed zithers of rich-honeyed wood.
There is a peacefulness to this place that soothes your crew, and they try to engage the musicians in conversation to learn more about their culture.
Attempt to hail them in their native tongue.

Your crew’s linguistic efforts attract much appreciative surprise, and a lively conversation soon sparks up, supplemented by voluminous approximative sign language and much laughter.
Before your sailors can object, an intricate tea set is brought out, and the small pewter cups are soon brimming with steaming, crisp-scented mint tea, supplemented by flavoursome pastries. Many tales are traded, and nightfall has long since passed when your crew return to the ship, arms laden with simple but intricate tokens of friendship.

Your crew barely knows enough of the language to greet the locals, let alone carry their questions. After a few long minutes of polite puzzlement, they courteously but pointedly turn away. Frustrated, your crew retreat to the ship, hoping the next port encountered will be slightly more cosmopolitan.
Gesticulate to try and convey your meaning.

Not wishing to interrupt the music, one sailor walks up to a man about to enter a nearby house and taps his shoulder to attract his attention. The man turns a curious face to this unexpected intervention.
Gesture between your mouth and the man, indicating you wish to speak to him.

The man’s face darkens with anger. He barks a few clearly offensive words and strides across the threshold, slamming the door in your crew’s baffled faces. Judging by the condemning stares they now attract, your sailors understand the gesture they made is considered a great insult, and wisely decide to retreat to the ship before committing another faux pas.
Point out the surroundings and give a thumbs up, indicating you find his home beautiful.

The man starts unpleasantly, visibly insulted, before casting a witheringly contemptuous glare at your expectant crew. Judging by the condemning stares they are suddenly attracting, your sailors understand the gesture must have some unknown, possibly derogatory meaning here, and wisely decide to retreat to the ship before committing another faux pas.
Place your hand on your heart to indicate you are glad to meet him.

The man smiles, and a conversation slowly begins, accompanied by a smattering of local idioms and considerable use of sign language. Understanding your crew to be foreign, he promptly invites them in and welcomes them with generous helpings of piping mint tea and soft, honeyed pastries.
When your crew part ways with him, they cannot help but feel comfort in the knowledge such friendships, beyond words and shared history, may still be found.

It is not long before your crew are hopelessly lost in the tangle of crowded streets. From all parts, merchants assail them with hopeful voices, flaunting the quality of their wares and the attractiveness of their prices in such a way that the sailors soon feel like a sloop buffeted by harsh winds.
One particularly bold and smiling merchant walks up to the lead sailor.
‘I have just the thing for you — rare items, impossible to find elsewhere!’
His wares seem common enough, but perhaps he can give you directions?
Try to secure his help by purchasing something.
Tahanina! You have an eye for fine items!
Accept
Cancel

The tradeoff hardly seems fair, but your sailors are eager to find a way out of the souq. Once the deal is concluded, the grinning merchant points them to a low set of arched doors nearby that will lead them back to the safety of the harbour.
Your crew try to convince themselves, loudly and unconvincingly, that the bauble will at least make for a decent souvenir, despite its hefty cost.

You try to haggle the prices down to something reasonable, but it becomes increasingly clear that the merchant has little intention of making an honest deal. This suspicion is confirmed when, after a particularly vehement refusal to pay a fortune for what looks like common kitchenware, he barks a few short words.
Immediately, several burly individuals appear through the draperies at the back of the shop. With a chill, you realise the price to pay has just increased steeply!
Relent and pay the price.
How pleasant to deal with reasonable people!
Accept
Cancel

The merchant can barely hide his glee as you hand over the outrageous fee he has just extorted from you. He waves a sardonic goodbye, as his acolytes lead your crew back through the crowded souq to the docks.
Once back aboard the ship, it becomes very tempting to throw the thing overboard, but the officers insist it be kept, tacking a note to it reading ‘Now you know why shore leave is restricted.’
Despite their valiant efforts, your men are severely trounced, and can barely make it back to the ship with their battered comrades before the whole town turns on them.
Object violently to this extortion.

Outnumbered though they may be, your sailors settle in for a fight, some of them drawing ribbing knives and various crude but wickedly-edged items from the pockets of their breeches. The thugs' faces fall, discountenanced by these weapons — evidently, they were not prepared for so hostile a reaction, and so safely back a few paces away, behind the dais.
Furious at his men’s cowardice, the merchant has no choice but to mumble directions to the harbour, leaving your crew to operate a swift retreat.

The battle that ensues is brief and bloody. Your men fight as valiantly as they can, but are swiftly overrun and turned out into the street, penniless and bloodied, where they regroup pitifully and hobble back to the ship as precipitously as they can.
Look away and plod onwards.

Not one to be so easily shaken off, the merchant steps into your crew’s footsteps, accusingly asking them if they are aware of how rude it is to ignore someone in such a fashion.
The ship’s boy rounds on him angrily.
‘Stop bein’ a bloody pain and scram!’
The man’s expression sours, and he steps forward and grabs the lad by the collar. Before anyone can react, your crew realize the altercation has attracted a crowd of hostile locals, some of them reaching for long knives.
Seize the merchant and use him as a shield.

One of your topmen leaps forward, twisting the merchant’s arm violently before pulling him in front to use as a shield.
There's a moment’s bated silence as the surrounding cut-throats hesitate, before rushing forward with a roar of outrage.
Outnumbered but well-versed in close-quarters combat, your crew throw the merchant into the charge, scattering the assailants, and promptly disarm and subdue their leaders.
Cowed and bruised, the thugs slink back to side streets, as your crew operate a hasty retreat to the safety of the ship.
Fearing for their lives, your crew have no choice but to flee to the ship, leaving the lad to bleed out on the dusty street.
Pay him. No amount of money is worth the lives of your crew.
Pay up now, or else.
Accept
Cancel

Fearing the result of a confrontation, the sailors fumble for some money, handing out various coins and valuables to the expectant merchant.
A quick command, and the ill-gotten treasure disappears into a worn-leather purse around the merchant’s neck. The man smirks, fingering his dagger ominously – much to the merriment of his henchmen.
Unwilling to tarry any longer, your crew turn heels and flee the scene, cheeks burning with the trailing sound of scornful hilarity.
Fearing for their lives, your crew have no choice but to flee to the ship, leaving the lad to bleed out on the dusty street.
Ignore his banter and ask him for directions.

Ignoring the outstretched wares, one of your sailors uses what little she knows of the local language to ask the man for the quickest path to the harbour.
He flounders, evidently conflicted, before mumbling a series of nigh-incomprehensible directions.
Your crew follow them as best they can, but whether due to their cryptic nature, or to your sailors’ general ineptitude in terms of orientation, it takes them the better part of the afternoon to find a way out of the souq and back onto the ship.
Examine the ragged men to find a suitable guide.

One of your crew members singles out a promising intellectual, with sleeves intricately patterned with dark arabesque lines. It is only when he eagerly draws nearer that you realise the lines are actually inked directly upon his skin — the verses of holy texts in his native script.

It is evident that he is well-learned despite his lowly means, and so helpful is he in describing the lore and history of the city that your diplomat cannot help but be impressed by his earnestness. When the time comes to pay him, your sailor instead offers him an apprenticeship, with your captain’s approval.The young man, however, is reticent, and claims his elderly family could not provide for itself without him.
Insist upon meeting his family in the hope of convincing them

The man’s home is barely more than a hovel, tucked away in an alcove on one of the narrower kuchehs threading the souq. His parents greet you worried, offering bland tea with oft-infused leaves, and it pains you to think it is probably the best they have to offer.
The debate is long and heated, with much arguing back and forth: the elderly couple are evidently worried as to their fate when they can no longer provide for themselves. However it is with a heavy heart that they ultimately relent and give him their blessing, imploring you to care for him as one of your own.

You follow the young man to a small, crowded room in one of the riads overlooking the market, where an aged couple greet you tersely. Their mood darkens as soon as they understand that you are asking to take their son away, and they firmly turn down your many arguments and offers.
‘The Book says the young must support the aged in the dusk of their life. Who are you to deny this?’ You think to reply that their son is no spring chicken himself, but
sensing their resolve, you have no choice but to relent and bid him a disappointed farewell.
Insist: such talent should not be wasted.

Flattered at first, the man soon wearies of your insistence.
‘I have duties here, and a family to care for. Your offer does you credit, but what are promises made by strangers newly met, however honourable, in the eyes of the duty imparted by the Almighty? My place is here.’
His tone as he finishes giving you a tour of the city is cooler, but when you part ways, he smiles, and you reward him generously for his expertise.
Respect his conviction and sense of duty.

No man should feel compelled to loftier destinies if their duty calls them elsewhere. Your crew compliment him on his sense of loyalty to his kin, and tip him handsomely for his guidance and company.
By way of a parting gift, he traces a few elegant lines on a small piece of paper — an errant verse from a poem he is working on — before disappearing back into the souq.
Roughly translated, the line reads ‘Mine was a life divinely ordained, and thus I knew serenity’, and is signed with the lad’s name, Qaddr Razzaq.

The men throng around you in a clamour of self-professed learnedness and helpfulness. Overwhelmed, you select a young man whose confidence and insistence seem to make him a wise option.
It is soon painfully obvious, however, that he was a poor choice. Though he does take you through the colourful and bustling souq, he has little to say about it, and his pace is brisk.
After an hour of so, you reach a remote and secluded part of the market, only to have him turn to you sombrely, declaring his guided tour complete and demanding an extortionate fee for his services.
Grit your teeth and pay the fee.
Surely you were not expecting my services to be free?
Accept
Cancel

Even a blatantly extortionate scheme such as this is better than risking being trapped in such an isolated part of town. Reluctantly, you hand over the hefty sum, and he deftly pockets it before disappearing into a nearby alley, leaving your crew to find their own way back to the ship — only now with lighter purses, and much animosity towards the locals.

Visibly upset at being denied his due, the young man starts chattering angrily in his native tongue. Your crew attempt to leave the place and find their own way back to the harbour through the stench of nearby tanneries, but your guide follows your every footstep, insisting upon being paid in increasingly loud and aggressive tones. You attempt to ignore him, but his relentlessness is sorely testing your crew's patience.
Attempt to intimidate and scare him away.

One of your sailors lashes out angrily at the young man, cuffing him sharply behind the head. ‘Learn your place, boy!’
He staggers slightly, dazed and shocked, terror welling up in his gaze. Before anyone can step in, he ducks behind a great vat of bubbling dyes and flees your sailors’ wrath.
While navigating a path back to the harbour, your crew cannot help but feel guilty at their treatment of the boy — when one is so abjectly destitute, it is little surprise that propriety should bow to need.

One of your sailors steps threateningly towards the boy, reaching out to grab him by the front of his ragged shirt. The lad, however, darts nimbly out of reach, colliding with another surprised sailor before leaping behind a high stratified stack of drying tea leaves. When your men round it, much to the protest of the labourers tending the stack, the lad has disappeared.
As your crew uncertainly head back to the harbour, the man the boy had run into cries out: his belt pouch is missing, evidently stolen!
The lad clearly needs to be taught the error of his ways.

‘It is natural that securing your basic needs should take precedence over your absolute moral being. But there are resources in the province of lawfulness that you could abide by...' and so on and so forth.
Your sailor’s benevolent, albeit pompous tones have some tempering effect on the lad, but when the lecture is over, you cannot help but wonder how much of it he understood, yet alone took to heart.

‘Never is there cause to be immoral, lest the principle of morality be neutered. If society is to be society and justice to be justice, there can be no legitimate unlawfulness, and consequently, you must reflect on your immorality and change your ways.’
The young man’s face darkens with every self-important word, and he swiftly turns heel on your sailor, stranding him mid-speech.
As your crew return to the ship, a series of angry mutterings arise from all parts, and a hail of broken earthenware rains down from high windows.
Your crew suffer numerous cuts and bruises.
Refuse to pay.
Medina of Al Souk
Head to Al Souk
Continue your journey
<font size='36'>With the hubbub and colour of the souk behind you, you wonder where to head next...</font>

The merchant scowls then clicks his tongue. One of the thugs promptly steps across the counter, landing a crashing blow onto one of your sailors.
The man collapses, out cold, and the frustration and anger that have been building up for the past hour burst into an all-out brawl — bloody business swiftly soured by the merchant’s cries for help, which draws in new foes by the minutes.
Your sailors’ efforts to intimidate the thugs backfires spectacularly when one them picks up a heavy-looking mattock from behind the counter and strikes out at the lead mariner.

Before you can act, the boy lashes out at the merchant, pushing him back into the crowd of his acolytes. With a roar, the merchant draws a cruel-looking knife from his belt and lunges at the boy.
The rest of the sailors try to intervene, but the attackers are too numerous — they push back your crew and surround the boy, shanking him viciously and repeatedly until his bloody corpse no longer moves.

Your crew hurry to pool whatever valuables they have, but the scowl on the merchant’s face only deepens when he glances at the handful of coins, clearly estimating it to be an unworthy price for the perceived offence.
He draws a cruel-looking knife from his belt and lunges at the boy, shanking him effortlessly.
The others try to intervene, but the henchmen easily push them back and surround the boy.
A Streetcar Named Olispo

The lights of Olispo glimmer through the spray as your sailors hasten to secure their mooring. Music and merriment spill from the narrow streets, wafting aromas of warm bread and savoury fish fresh from the tide.
With a thrill of pent up anticipation, the sailors stream off the ship and excitedly crowd onto a pristinely new yellow tram, laughing as it rickets off into the warm night, hailed loudly by festive locals.
A flurry of ample sleeves turns to them genially:
'Boa noite, friends! From whence does the tide bring you?'
Lie: 'We hail from Il Campanile'

‘Maravilhoso! I have kin there — wonderful people, and hardworking to a fault!
Come, we must drink — and I know just the place. Follow me!’
The sailors clamber off the tram gracelessly, unaccustomed to its peculiar rhythm, before following the man through a maze of passages lit by antique oil lamps hanging from balconies. Stopping before a low stone arch, he reaches through the overgrown ivy, pulling open an unseen door.
A flare of chattering and low lights greets you, wafting dark-scented spirits and fresh-roasted food.‘Try the pasteis de nata, our sweet, secret custardy pride! And of course, our famous port!'
Order a generous round of port and custard pies
Any friend of José's is a friend of mine!
Accept
Cancel

The innkeeper navigates the thronged room expertly, avoiding boisterous patrons to set a large platter onto the table. Your crew swiftly attack the warm pastries, wolfing down the soft custard with aplomb, while Jose introduces a merry waltz of friends, each eager to toast the newcomers to their city.
When the festivities peter out in the late hours of the night, your sailors trickle back the ship, full-bellied, light-headed and free of care.

The innkeeper scoffs when your crew remark on the price.
‘This is no mere city, amigos. This is Olispo, land of riches and flavour! Surely you do not expect to feast for free!’
There's a minute of long, awkward silence before Jose, obviously crestfallen, clears his throat. Clearly, he had hoped his helpfulness would earn him a night of free food and drink.
With a curt bow and a ‘Boa noite’, he steps out into the night.
Suddenly the crowd seems much less amicable, and you cannot help but wonder how deep into the city your guide has taken you. A hasty retreat is swiftly declared.
Climb back onto the tram

The yellow tram lurches into movement, starting its trundling jaunt down the street. Suddenly, a cry rings out: an ornate horse-drawn carriage is hurtling towards the crossing! The look of terror on the coachman’s face makes it clear he has lost control of the horse.
With a shudder, the tram stops not three feet from the carriage, startling the creature to a halt. Terrified, it rears impossibly high, its hooves crashing down inches from the carriage.
There is a strange, garbled cry, and a man’s face appears at the window, livid, and with top hat askew, pleading for help.
Attempt to calm the horse

A wisp of a girl, only recently part of the crew, sets her face resolutely and edges forward, whispering words of comfort to the panicked creature. Her hand extends to the horse’s chin, turning its eyes away from the metallic sheen of the tram and towards the soft light of a nearby street. Slowly, the animal stills.
The door to the carriage creaks open and a pale man steps uncertainly out. He straightens, and looks at the gathered sailors hazily before paying a low bow, sweeping the dusty street with his top hat.
‘My name is Vasco Oliveira, and in the name of King Joao of Olispo, whom it is my privilege to serve, I pray you accept this small token of thanks.’

A short, thick-eyed man hesitates, then inches forward to calm the horse — albeit to no avail. It tosses and whinnies furiously, battering the street and rails in a series of metallic clangs which only exacerbates its terror.
A sudden fear gleams in its eye — the carriage lurches into a mad gallop, running over your sailor with a sickening crack and streaming off into the night.
Your surgeon's wounds are serious and must be tended to at once. Heavy-hearted, your crew carry their suffering comrade back to the ship.
Cut the carriage reins

A lanky young topman swiftly reaches into his coat for a carving knife and leaps forward. There's a flash of metal and a snap of leather before the coachman topples back into his seat. The horse whinnies and heads off down the street at a gallop, scaring passersby out of the way. As it rounds the corner, it bowls over a young girl, sending her barrelling into a pile of glaring, dead-eyed, cod, which collapses on her.
However, only then do you remember the stricken cry you heard from inside the carriage.
Rush to the girl’s aid

A woman with medical knowledge rushes to the girl and kneels by her side.
Pulling her deftly out of the pile of odorous fish, she quickly realizes the girl’s right arm is broken, along with possibly two of her ribs.
She commands some strips of wood and cloth be brought to her, and binds the girl's arm and chest as tightly as possible. It will do until the girl is seen to by more experienced hands.
As the girl's mother steps in to help her daughter up, she insists upon rewarding your crew for their selflessness.

Emboldened, a sailor leaps off the tram and rushes to help the girl up.. Pain flashes across her face, but your man finds no trace of injury.
‘Why the theatrics, darling?’ he chuckles.
Infuriated, the girl’s mother steps in, shoving the sailor aside.
‘Are you mad, woman?’ he exclaims angrily,
grabbing the girl's arm, intent on proving her health, but a mountain of man steps out from the gathering crowd and deftly locks him in a tight hold.
'Time you left Olispo, senhor...'
His elaborate moustache quivers with repressed anger as he releases his victim and sees you threateningly off into the night.
Rush to the carriage door

One of your crew rushes to the door, swinging it open to reveal a tall man in a ruffled frock coat and top hat. He is unhurt and courteously refuses the outstretched hand to step out of the carriage, taking a deep, steadying breath to gather his composure.
‘A fine show of valour, if perhaps somewhat foolhardy; events might have unfurled very differently. Nevertheless, you succeeded, and for this,’ he doffs his hat to the assembled sailors, bowing low, ‘I, Vasco Oliveira, am much obliged to you.’
Surely you don’t mean Oliveira, the ambassador to King João?

‘The very same, and much honoured to be known by your company! It seems not so long ago I journeyed with some of your countrymen. Pray, do not be startled: it is a small feat indeed for a diplomat such as myself to recognise your accent. I recall your countrymen as amiable fellows, and though we had our differences, we parted in good fellowship.'
He walks to the back of the carriage and opens the trunk.
'Please, accept this small trinket for the sake of better days and friendships not forgotten.’
Oliveira? Are you perhaps Vicente Silva’s cousin?

A barely hidden scowl flashes across his face.
‘Vicente is my cousin, yes, although why anyone would want to be acquainted with that imbecil is beyond me.' He gives you a cursory glance. I thank you for your efforts, but perhaps it is better that we do not associate any further — clearly you know my cousin too much already.'
With the curtest of bows, he turns away and makes for the fallen girl nearby.
Faces flushed with being publicly dismissed, your crew swiftly head back to the harbour, cursing the fickleness of technology and gentility alike.
Sure not the Oliveira whose paintings are of notoriously exquisite detail?

He draws himself up haughtily, his pride evidently pricked.
‘I believe you must be confusing me with the Marques de Oliveira, Adao. A tolerable mistake, had he not been dead twenty years. If you will excuse me, I have matters of a very much living nature to attend to.'
He turns to the coachman, barking a few commands before stepping back into the coach. Already the tale of the foreigners who couldn't tell the living from the dead is spreading like wildfire in not-so-discreet mutterings. This is not what the captain had in mind when he bid you make the Empire proud.
Return to the ship

Time has flown unheeded, and already the hour grows late. The tide waits for no man — nor, for that matter, do the ships’ officers. Your crew drain their last drinks then make their way slowly back to the harbour and the relative comfort of their berths.

When dawn breaks upon the sleeping city, the ship is already picking up speed, its sails taught with the promise of new journeys.
Refuse to order

José casts a disappointed glance upon your crew.
‘I had hoped that seamen would be more adventurous. You would insult us by refusing bread and wine offered in the spirit of friendship? Or are you simply too close-minded?’ He scoffs. ‘You can find your own way out, I am sure.’
Before any of your crew can object, he swivels and disappears into the crowd.
Determined not to conclude the evening on so dispiriting an encounter, you head back to the tram and ride it through the city, back to the harbour through the most circuitous route available, enthusiastically remarking upon the wonders of the modern age between every clank and rumble of the car.

Your attempts at a Campanilese accent draw a few laughs from surrounding passengers, but the man's insistence on making broken conversation soon becomes trying for all.
One of your men mutters something about him minding his own bloody business — 'don't you have some goats to adopt?'
The native's face flares with fury, rounding on the sulking sailor and answering in your own tongue. 'I tried, but your Queen already has Sir Archibald.'
There is a stunned silence in the tramcar while your crew reel with shock and disgust, before a thick-set young lass leans in and knees him heavily in the midriff, sending him tumbling into a crowd of his outraged countrymen.
For Queen and country!'

A roar of approval rises from your men as the man sinks to the floor, crimson-faced and groaning. Several burly moustachioed passengers leap into the fray, belts wrapped around their fists, only to be tripped and set upon viciously by sailors eager to vent weeks' worth of restlessness. A whistle sounds through the haze of torn upholstery - the local constabulary!
Your crew promptly jump down from the tram, with a flurry of jabs for good measure, and disperse into the surrounding streets.

A tram hardly makes for a convenient battle ground. Fists fly into errant faces, drawing bystanders into the brawl and ruining the plush new upholstery. When the coachman finally pulls abruptly on the brakes, sending everyone to the floor, the tramcar more closely resembles a dog-fighting pit than a coach.
Your crew scarper, dispersing through the streets with the shrill whistles of the constabulary hot on their tails. Some are dragged off for a night of holding, and the prospect of public disgrace in the morning.
This is a fight we cannot hope to win

A wise person chooses their fights carefully — and a sailor, expected to report to duty on the morrow, wounded or not, doubly so.
Your crew hastily disembark from the tramcar, stumbling onto the street, and march back to their fallen comrade, ignoring the jeers and heckling of passengers roused by their aggressor’s anger.
The walk back to the ship seems interminable, and though all agree to turn in for an early night, the gloom of the abandoned festivities hangs heavy in your crew’s heart until the late hours of the night.
We serve Her Majesty'

The Empire, eh? It is fortunate you have come on this day, for we are not by nature a forgiving people, and there is much history between us — most of it written in blood. But let us speak no more of this: tonight, we feast and revel; tonight we look to the future! See how swiftly the world changes — why, not a decade ago who would have imagined a tram here? Aye, in years past we drew blood, but tonight we draw wine, and drink to hope, and progress! What say you, por Deus?'
His hearty enthusiasm appears genuine, but you cannot help but wonder how deeply these past grievances are truly buried.
‘Let the strife of our parents die with them, then. To your good health!'

A beaming smile lights up his face.
‘Otimo! To a better world, and the bittersweet promise of peace. Let not our forebears cast long shadows over us — to peace!’
He seems to come upon a sudden idea. ‘My name is Alexio, and you must dine with me tonight! We have prepared food aplenty — the finest fare and freshest fish in the entire city, upon my word! Surely you will join us? Such a feast is best shared, and you would be most welcome! It is not every day our city gets its first tram!’
Gladly! To the feast!'

Alexio takes your eager crew through the streets of Olispo, skilfully weaving in and out of bustling crowds. Torches dance on the azulejos, a strange hypnotic flickering that makes the houses and high walls seem alive with warm, gay colours.
Everywhere, the sounds of chattering laughter, glasses clinking and food being shared fills the air.
A low-hanging door opens onto a bustling taberna — ‘Alexio, at last! We feared the port would run out before you arrived!’
Good cheer lasts well into the night, and dawn finds your crew rich with bonds newly tempered by joyous drinking, and the promise of a brighter future.
Not tonight, friend. The first mate's particular about early rising'

Obviously crestfallen, but determined to be amicable, Alexio helps the crew navigate a path through the crowds back to the harbour before taking his leave with a wave of his hand. He soon melts back into the throng.
As the last of the crew fall asleep in their berths, they can still hear the din of celebration in the distance, extending well into the small hours of the night.
War is the province of kings, and we will not be pawns in their games'

He scowls, angrily. ‘What do you know of war, of sacrifice and duty? Many of my kin perished in what you call a game, for what they believed was right.’ His raised voice draws the attention of other patrons, their faces souring as they understand the tenor of the argument. ‘A man's land is his blood, the word of his king his command. I pity you that you cannot understand that.'
He spits contemptuously at your feet, then vanishes into the throng before any retribution can be exacted.
The silence left in his wake is ominous with untold resentment. You try to order a round of port, but the inkeep stares you out of the door.
Only when Olispo has answered for its crimes will we have peace.'

He bows his head grimly. ‘Foul are the tides of war, and gore-hungry its hounds — none who spill blood can lay claim to righteousness. There are horrors in the past of both our nations. Yet is it not for we who follow to strive to be better? If we can, you and I, have a civil conversation, then perhaps there is still hope for friendship in our nations?
Vamos, let us extend Olispo's hospitality to you, and meet today as brothers rather than foes. To modernity, and peace!’
A noble offer, and one we are glad to accept!

Alexio takes your eager crew through the streets of Olispo, skilfully weaving in and out of the bustling crowds. Torches and gaslights dance on the azulejos, a strange hypnotic flickering that makes the houses and high walls seem alive with warm, gay colours.
Everywhere, the sound of chattering laughter, glasses clinking against each other and food being shared fills the air.
A low-hanging door opens onto a bustling taberna – ‘Alexio, at last! We feared the port would run out before you arrived!’

Not tonight, friend; duty calls, and rest

As the last of the crew fall asleep in their berths, they can still hear the din of celebration in the distance, extending well into the small hours of the night.
